Simulate competing risks data

Source: R/sim_cmprsk.R
sim_cmprsk.Rd

Simulates right-censored competing risks data with baseline numerical covariates (up to 10 features) and a specified number of competing event causes (2 to 5). Event times and causes are generated from cause-specific Weibull proportional hazards. Censoring times are generated independently from a Weibull distribution.

Usage

sim_cmprsk(
  n,
  n_features = 3L,
  n_causes = 2L,
  event_probs = NULL,
  shape = 1,
  rate = 0.2,
  beta_sd = 0.3
)

Arguments

n

(integer(1))
Positive number of observations (sample size), should be at least n_causes.

n_features

(integer(1))
Number of independent features drawn from the standard normal distribution, from 1 to 10. Defaults to 3.

n_causes

(integer(1))
Number of competing event causes, from 2 to 5. Defaults to 2.

event_probs

(numeric() | NULL)
Desired observed cause probabilities, in cause order, with length n_causes. Every entry must be finite and strictly positive, and their sum must not exceed 1. The remaining probability specifies censoring; a sum of 1 disables censoring. These probabilities hold theoretically when beta_sd = 0, and are approximate with covariate effects. NULL uses rep(0.8 / n_causes, n_causes), targeting 20% censoring and dividing the remaining 80% equally among the competing causes when beta_sd = 0.

shape

(numeric(1))
Positive, finite common Weibull shape for event and censoring times. Defaults to 1, giving constant hazards and exponentially distributed times.

rate

(numeric(1))
Positive, finite multiplier for the baseline cumulative hazards, defaulting to 0.2. Cause-specific coefficients are rate * event_probs, and the censoring coefficient is rate * (1 - sum(event_probs)). Larger values produce shorter times without changing the theoretical event and censoring proportions.

beta_sd

(numeric(1))
Nonnegative, finite standard deviation of the normal regression coefficients. Defaults to 0.3; zero disables covariate effects.

Value

A data.table with n rows and the following columns:

  • time: positive, finite observed time \(T_i\).

  • event: integer observed event code, with 0 for censoring and 1 through n_causes for competing events.

  • x1, ..., xp: baseline features, where p = n_features.

  • event_time, event_cause: latent first event time \(Y_i\) and cause \(J_i\).

  • cens_time: independent censoring time \(C_i\), or Inf when censoring is disabled.

  • total_rate: total individual event cumulative-hazard coefficient \(R_i\), excluding censoring.

  • lp1, ..., lpK: cause-specific linear predictors \(x_i^\top \beta_k\), where K = n_causes.

  • rate1, ..., rateK: individual cause-specific cumulative-hazard coefficients \(r_{ik}\).

Details

For each observation \(i\), the baseline covariates \(x_i\) are independent standard normal variables. Each cause \(k = 1, \ldots, K\) has a coefficient vector \(\beta_k\), whose elements are independently sampled from \(N(0, \mathrm{beta\_sd}^2)\).

The cause-specific hazards follow a Weibull proportional hazards model:

$$h_{ik}(t) = \gamma \lambda_k t^{\gamma - 1} \exp(x_i^\top \beta_k),$$

where \(\gamma = \mathrm{shape} > 0\) is the common Weibull shape and \(\lambda_k = \mathrm{rate} \cdot p_k > 0\) is the cause-specific baseline cumulative-hazard coefficient. The \(p_k\) are the specified target proportions for the observed competing events. With shape = 1 (the default), the hazards are constant over time and event times follow exponential distributions.

Define \(r_{ik} = \lambda_k \exp(x_i^\top \beta_k)\) and \(R_i = \sum_{k=1}^K r_{ik}\). The cumulative hazards and overall event-free survival function, conditional on the covariates, are

$$H_{ik}(t) = r_{ik} t^\gamma, \qquad H_i(t) = R_i t^\gamma,$$

$$S_i(t) = \exp(-R_i t^\gamma).$$

The quantities \(r_{ik}\) and \(R_i\) are cumulative-hazard coefficients, corresponding to constant hazard rates when \(\gamma = 1\).

To simulate the uncensored event time, draw \(E_i \sim \mathrm{Exp}(1)\) and set

$$Y_i = (E_i / R_i)^{1/\gamma}.$$

The event cause \(J_i\) is then sampled with probabilities \(P(J_i = k \mid x_i) = r_{ik}/R_i\). Because all cause-specific hazards share the same Weibull shape, the event cause and uncensored event time are conditionally independent given the covariates. This follows the cause-specific hazard-based simulation framework of Beyersmann et al. (2009).

Censoring is generated independently of the covariates and event process. Let \(p_0 = 1 - \sum_{k=1}^K p_k\) and \(\lambda_C = \mathrm{rate} \cdot p_0\). Draw \(E_{Ci} \sim \mathrm{Exp}(1)\) independently and set

$$C_i = (E_{Ci} / \lambda_C)^{1/\gamma}.$$

If \(p_0 = 0\), set \(C_i = \infty\), corresponding to no censoring. The observed time is \(T_i = \min(Y_i, C_i)\), with observed event indicator \(\delta_i = J_i\) if \(Y_i \le C_i\), and \(\delta_i = 0\) otherwise.

Under this model, the cause-specific cumulative incidence functions have the analytical form

$$F_{ik}(t) = \frac{r_{ik}}{R_i} \left(1 - \exp(-R_i t^\gamma)\right),$$

satisfying \(\sum_{k=1}^K F_{ik}(t) = 1 - S_i(t)\).

The conditional probability of observing cause \(k\) is \(r_{ik}/(R_i + \lambda_C)\), while the probability of censoring is \(\lambda_C/(R_i + \lambda_C)\). Thus, event_probs gives the exact theoretical marginal proportions (\(p_k\) and \(p_0\) respectively) when beta_sd = 0. With covariate effects, these are only nominal targets. Realized sample proportions also vary due to random sampling.

The function errors if any cause is missing among the observed events, and reports the missing causes. Missing causes are more likely with small samples, rare causes, or heavy censoring, so try to adjust n, event_probs, or n_causes if necessary. Extreme parameter values producing invalid rates or event times also can result in an error.

Use set.seed() for reproducibility.

References

Beyersmann, Jan, Latouche, Aurelien, Buchholz, Anika, Schumacher, Martin (2009). “Simulating competing risks data in survival analysis.” Statistics in Medicine, 28(6), 956–971. doi:10.1002/sim.3516 .

Examples

set.seed(42)
data = sim_cmprsk(200, n_features = 5L, n_causes = 3L, event_probs = c(0.4, 0.2, 0.1))
